In the modern Java ecosystem, application packaging has evolved far beyond the classic split-archive model of standalone WARs or directories of loose JAR files deployed to external servlet containers. A fat JAR, commonly referred to as an executable JAR, solves the fundamental deployment friction of shipping an enterprise application by packaging the compiled bytecode, all transitive third-party dependencies, and an embedded HTTP server into a single, self-contained archive file. Instead of maintaining complex classpath strings or managing disparate container versions on target servers, an executable JAR allows operators to spin up an entire enterprise service using a simple java -jar command.

However, naively packing thousands of external dependency JARs inside a single fat archive introduces severe operational inefficiencies, particularly in containerized environments like Docker and Kubernetes. Because a standard fat JAR places every library flat inside a nested directory structure (such as BOOT-INF/lib in Spring Boot), any modification to a single line of application source code alters the checksum of the entire archive, forcing container build pipelines to invalidate the cache and re-upload gigabytes of unchanged library layers. To mitigate this, modern build tools implement layers, a structural packaging strategy that segregates application binaries from stable third-party dependencies. By breaking down the fat JAR into distinct physical tiers—dependencies, snapshot dependencies, resources, and application classes—container engines can cache underlying layers independently. When code changes occur, only the lightweight application binary layer is rebuilt and pushed to the registry, dramatically accelerating CI/CD pipelines and reducing storage overhead.

items: An executable JAR relies on a custom Main-Class entry in its META-INF/MANIFEST.MF file, usually pointing to a JarLauncher or PropertiesLauncher provided by frameworks like Spring Boot rather than the user's actual application entry point.

The custom launcher bootstraps a specialized classloader (like LaunchedURLClassLoader) capable of navigating nested JAR archives (JAR-within-JAR) without requiring the JVM to fully unpack dependency archives to the host file system.
Layering relies on a metadata descriptor (e.g., layers.idx) that explicitly instructs the packaging tool which classpath entries belong to specific physical tiers during the archive assembly phase.

When running in a container, tools like Docker utilize the layered structure via multi-stage builds, copying dependencies, spring-boot-loader classes, and application snapshots in separate Dockerfile RUN COPY directives to maximize layer reuse.

spring-boot-maven-plugin configuration for explicit layer indexing:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <layers>
            <enabled>true</enabled>
            <configuration>${project.basedir}/src/layers.xml</configuration>
        </layers>
    </configuration>
</plugin>

A common production gotcha when working with executable fat JARs and layers involves memory mapping and file descriptor exhaustion. Because nested JARs are often read dynamically or extracted to the system temp directory (/tmp) by certain container runtimes or older framework launchers, ensure that your container environment has sufficient /tmp storage and that you monitor open file descriptors to prevent JVM crashes under heavy classloading concurrency.
